newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION-FY98 BUDGET PREVIEW - By J.M. Share & Stock Brokers.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-FY98 BUDGET PREVIEW - By J.M. Share & Stock Brokers.

text.p: The following is an excerpt from a pre-budget analysis
by securities firm J.M. Share & Stockbrokers
"FISCAL PRUDENCE" Versus "POLITICAL DURESS":

The task of the Finance Minister has been well and truly cut out. When P. Chidambaram rises to present the FY 97/98 Union Budget on Feburary 28, he will have to give away the contradictions that would have gone into the preparation of the Budget.

Undoubtedly, political pressures and coalition constraints would have brought in their own brand of 'short-termism' and come in the way of balancing the budget. The FM could not have possibly avoided all those pulls in toto, but he would have done enough if his Budget:
** desisted from achieving that much extolled shibboleth of 'fiscal consolidation' at the expense of declining support for the Plan outlay and
** rekindled confidence in the investment environment.
And in that case, the equity markets should witness a rerating.

Notwithstanding all these hurdles, we believe that the FM will balance the Budget at a fiscal deficit of around 4.5 percent of GDP and a revenue deficit of 2.3 percent in FY 97/98. But before our expectations from the forthcoming budget, a look at the deviations that we are projecting for FY96/97.
FY 96/97 JM ESTIMATES INDICATE A FAMILIAR SLIP IN FISCAL DEFICIT:

** We are estimating a shortfall of 31,600 million rupees in tax and non-tax revenue receipts for the Centre, relative to the budgeted figures. The below par collection is on account of shortfall in all the major taxes save individual and the non-realisation of the budgeted telecom license fees. Blame lower corporate profitability, lower industrial production, lower import growth (perversely even an overvalued exchange rate) for the mishap on the tax front.
** PSU disinvestment for garnering 50,000 million rupees has been a non-starter, IOC certainly won't happen this fiscal, VSNL possibly could collect 5,000 million rupees.
** Interim Pay relief will absorb only 15,000 million rupees of Fifth Pay Commission, but non-plan expenditure excluding this provisioning should exceed budget target by 30,000 million rupees.

** The Government's market borrowing programme has been the biggest beneficiary of poor non-food credit offtake and the string of CRR cuts. Centre's net borrowing programme is estimated to surpass budget target by 10,600 million rupees. We don't expect the Government to announce any fresh auction following that of the 10,000 million rupees long bond auction on February 20 (budget deficit might however set the Government thinking).

** Though budget deficit in FY 96/97 will widen considerably due to shortfall in overall receipts and an increase in expenditure (excluding pay provision), fiscal deficit will remain in the vicinity of 5.5 percent of GDP. However, we won't be surprised if this figure turns out to be lower due to an axe on plan expenditure (so, look at the revenue deficit). Doesn't the lack of aggregate demand suggest a cut in plan outlay?.
ACCOMPLISHMENT OF AMBITIOUS FY 97/98 FISCAL TARGETTING CONTINGENT ON PICKUP IN AGGREGATE DEMAND:
First an outline of policy changes expected -
MACROECONOMIC:
** Replacement of Ad hocs by Ways and Means Advances:

The RBI's proposal to replace Ad hocs with Ways and Means Advances should most probably be implemented in the budget. The basic difference with the WMA, as opposed to Ad hocs, is that it provides an overdraft facility for meeting the temporary mismatch between Government receipts and expenditure without being a permanent source of financing. The maximum budgetary gap that emerges as a result of the seasonal characteristics could be deemed to be the overdraft limit for the Centre. What the WMA will do is make life easier as far as monetary policy for the RBI is concerned.
** Time table for Convertibility:

We expect the Budget to recast FERA (continuance of restrictions is based on unfounded fears) and set up the base for a phased convertibility programme (can't think it would be in one go). We are convinced that full convertibility will not result in what has become a favourite cliche - 'forex disaster'. Wating for inflation or fiscal deficit to be reigned in is a nice-nellyism for saying 'no conver-tibility.
** Freeing of the Insurance Sector:

The magnitude of the infrastructure requirements that have been enumerated in the Expert Group's recommendations calls for increasing domestic savings considerably. Household savings need to be boosted by channelising an increasing volume into long term debt instruments and into contractual savings such as life insurance, pension and provident funds. A monolith insurance sector prevents optimal savings targetting and the time is ripe for announcing specific guidelines for opening of the sector to private participants.
** Specific Implementation of the Expert Group recommendations:
The Group has recommended a host of measures to tackle India's appaling infrastructure by setting up a simple regulatory mechanism:
++ fiscal incentives for equity investments - tax reliefs from the erstwhile 80CC provision for investments in long-gestation projects.
++ allowing entry of new private and public Provident Funds along with deployment guidelines based on prudential norms.

++ kickstarting of the debt market by removing existing impediments - create sovereign yield curve, remove pre-emptions on interbank borrowings, reintroduce repos transactions, institutional finance for debt market intermediaries and issue of tax-free bonds by private sector infrastructure companies.
DIRECT AND INDIRECT TAX RELATED:
** MAT will persist in some form or the other:

The villain of the secondary equity markets in FY 96/97 will continue to be a part of the corporate tax structure in FY 97/98. With direct taxes as a proportion of GDP being a mere 3 percent, the Government does not have many options. However, exports given their strategic importance in the overall Balance of Payments might come off Minimum Alternative Tax. Ideally, we would recommend the introduction of a Minimum Advance Tax, credit for which could be claimed in the future years. We submit that a realignment of depreciation norms to integrate tax and Company's Act regulations (reducing the former) could crush existing sentiment and spark off a massive selloff.
** Corporate Surcharge tax should make an exit, Hope only for first slab direct tax payers:

We expect the 7.5 percent surcharge on corporate taxes to be removed, bringing the marginal tax rate to 40 percent. Our proxy effective corporate tax rate for FY 96/97 which is estimated to be 29.5 percent will consequently fall to 27.4 percent in FY 97/98. Though there has been a lot of clamour for reduction in the overall taxation rate to 35 percent, we are not too sure how the FM would accede to such a request. With most states reeling under fiscal distress, there is not going to be much relief for the individual tax payers - First slab might have a reduced tax rate (10 percent), standard deduction might be increased at best to 18,000 rupees. Probably one of the two will happen.
** Average Import tariff rate should fall:

In FY 96/97, the imposition of the 2 percent special import duty increased average tariff rate. in the next fiscal, we expect overall import tariff to come off by 2 percent from an estimated 29 percent in FY 96/97. Domestic industries crying for protection (not entirely unfounded) will have to draw solace from a depreciated rupee. The Exim Policy will carry the trade liberalisation further by transferring several goods into the SIL and OGL categories.
CAPITAL MARKET RELATED:
The equity markets are banking on:
* the scrapping of double taxation on dividends
* the introduction of the buyback facility of shares for
corporates to shore up sentiment and
* the entry of Providend Funds into the equity market.
While we think that the first 2 measures might materialise, PFs as a preliminary step might be allowed to invest in triple rated corporate debt with an aim to increase investor returns.

Debt markets - FIIs seeking investment in gilt and corporate securities are confronted currently with a withholding tax of 20 percent. It is quite incongruous for an investor taking a currency risk to be paying up the withholding tax and for an investor isolated from currency risk (as in case of ECBs) to be paying none. The FM will most probably address this anomaly.
Summation of FY 97/98 budgeted numbers:

We have balanced the budget at a fiscal deficit equivalent to 4.6 percent of GDP. We are estimating the budget size to register a 13.6 percent increase over our revised FY 96/97 figures, with plan expenditure slated to move up by 10 percent. The non-plan expenditure consists of abundant provisoning for the fifth Pay Commission recommendations (50,000 million rupees) and the return of 44,400 million rupees to the Oil Coordination Committee. The FM is unlikely to mix the bad news with the good news and announce a fuel price hike. On the receipts side, we are projecting an 18.8 percent growth in tax and non-tax receipts and are also assuming a 6,000 rupees collection via PSU disinvestment (something that has not happened in the last 2 fiscal years). Further, we expect the Government's net market borrowing programme at 275,000 million rupees to exceed that of FY 96/97.
IMPACT ON EQUITY MARKETS:

In the light of the expected budget proposals and fiscal numbers, what sort of picture are we painting for equity markets? The equity markets in anticipation of the goodies have already climbed over 3500 levels and are trading in a valuation band of 10.3-10.6 (x) our FY 97/98 estimated earnings. Our belief is that the market is trading at the upper end of its valuation range, given current sentiment. The impending fuel hike and poor FY 96/97 corporate results (one might say that the world knows it, but we know that when the actual bitter news arrives, there is a 'Moment and Truth') might provide better entry points into the market. Further, with FII investments to be swayed by the corporate cash call in the GDR market during the next six months, demand in the secondary market could be hampered. As it is, net FII inflows for the first six weeks of FY 96/97 have been a mere USD 120 million. Our conclusion is that at present valuations, the market is a trader's market and could well be that way during 1H'1997.
(The opinions expressed in this article reflect the views of the author only. They should not be taken as reflecting the views of Reuters)
